objection: Was Jesus made God at the Council of Nicaea?
answer:
This objection deserves a real answer rather than dismissal, because the historical claim it makes—that Nicaea *formulated* rather than *received* a doctrine—is precisely what the evidence contradicts. The word homoousios is indeed extra-biblical, but the framers of Nicaea never pretended otherwise; they coined a technical term to *fence* a conviction already ancient, against Arius's novel claim that "there was when He was not." That's the key point: Arius was the innovator, not the bishops. His view had followers, yes, but it had to argue against an already-entrenched worship of Christ as God—worship attested from outside the church itself, as when Pliny the Younger reports Christians around AD 112 singing hymns to Christ "as to a god," decades before any council existed.

On the New Testament side, the confession of Jesus as Lord and God is not a late layer but embedded in its earliest strata—material predating Paul's own letters—and Matthew 28:19 already binds Father, Son, and Spirit into a single divine name at the Great Commission itself. Modern historical scholarship on early Jewish Christian devotion confirms this: worship of Jesus alongside the Father erupted within the first years among Jewish believers, using precisely the markers—Creator, bearer of the divine Name, recipient of prayer—by which Judaism guarded God's uniqueness. So Deuteronomy 6:4 and John 17:3 are not embarrassments to Trinitarian faith; they're its starting point. The doctrine says God is one in essence, and that this one God's identity includes Father, Son, and Spirit—not three gods, and not a later philosophical graft, but the earliest confession straining for adequate words. Nicaea supplied the word three centuries later because Arius forced the technical question; it didn't supply the faith.

I appreciate the chance to raise this—it's central to why many of us doubt the traditional Trinity doctrine.

The Council of Nicaea in 325 AD didn't discover a doctrine that was already plainly taught in Scripture; it *formulated* it, under political pressure from Constantine. Before Nicaea, the church debated seriously whether the Son was created (*Arius's* view had real followers), and afterward, the bishops officially *defined* Jesus as "of one substance" (*homoousios*) with the Father—language you won't find in the Bible itself. If the Trinity were as clear in the apostles' writings as Trinitarians claim, why did it take three centuries, a Roman emperor's interference, and a council vote to settle it? Deuteronomy 6:4 and John 17:3 teach monotheism plainly; the doctrine that God is three persons in one essence looks far more like a philosophical imposition on Scripture than a faithful echo of what Jesus and the apostles actually taught.
